They only acted after being publicly exposed - where was this 'commitment to ethics' before the documentary? The $25M fund sounds impressive but could easily be a tax write-off compared to their profits from these unethical practices. I'd need to see sustained action over years, not weeks, before considering any relationship with them again.

This response actually increases my trust relative to where it would be with a typical defensive corporate statement. The speed, specificity, and financial commitment suggest genuine accountability rather than damage control. However, my overall trust is still damaged - excellent crisis response doesn't erase the fact that these supply chain failures happened under their watch. As an ESG fund manager, I'd move them from 'hold' to 'watch closely' pending the audit results, but wouldn't divest immediately given their response quality.

Honestly, I'm torn. On one hand, they're doing all the right things - taking responsibility, spending real money, bringing in outside auditors. But the speed of this response makes me wonder if they knew about these problems already and had a crisis plan ready to go. I shop with brands I trust, and this shakes that foundation even if they're handling it well. I'd probably wait to see those weekly updates and the audit results before deciding whether to keep buying from them.

My trust remains fundamentally unchanged - this is textbook crisis management, not genuine transformation. The speed and polish of this response suggests they had contingency plans ready, which raises questions about what they knew and when. As a journalist, I'd be more interested in tracking their actual implementation over the coming months rather than taking these promises at face value. The real story will be whether they follow through on the weekly updates and whether that Deloitte audit has genuine independence.

While this response demonstrates appropriate accountability and swift action, my trust would remain conditional pending verification of implementation. The 90-day timeline concerns me - comprehensive supply chain audits typically require 6-12 months for thoroughness. I'd need to see the actual audit scope, Deloitte's methodology, and whether the Chief Supply Chain Ethics Officer has genuine independence and authority. The weekly progress updates are promising for transparency, but I'll be watching closely for substantive compliance measures rather than public relations gestures.

Honestly, this response makes me feel more conflicted than anything. On one hand, I'm relieved they're taking swift action and being transparent - that's exactly what I'd want to see as an employee. But I'm also worried about what this means for our company's reputation and ultimately my job security. The fact that we had these supply chain issues in the first place makes me question how well our leadership really knew what was happening, even though I generally trust them.

As a competitor analyst, this response actually reinforces my view that EcoHarvest has strong crisis management capabilities - which makes them a more formidable competitor, not less. The speed and comprehensiveness suggests they've learned from other companies' mistakes and had protocols ready. However, the real test will be execution and whether they can maintain this transparency momentum beyond the initial crisis period. From a strategic standpoint, their willingness to invest $25M and undergo public auditing could set new industry standards that smaller competitors will struggle to match.

My trust remains fundamentally damaged. While the response demonstrates some accountability, the speed suggests they knew about these issues beforehand - which raises serious questions about their commitment to transparency. The choice of Deloitte for the audit is problematic given potential consulting conflicts that could compromise independence. I'd need to see the actual audit methodology and whether truly independent bodies are involved before considering any restoration of credibility. Actions like these feel more like damage control than genuine ethical commitment.

This response actually increases my confidence in EcoHarvest as an investment prospect, despite the initial violations. The speed and comprehensiveness of their crisis management demonstrates institutional maturity and suggests they have robust governance frameworks already in place. However, my trust remains conditional - the real test will be execution quality and whether the Deloitte audit reveals systemic issues or isolated failures. The $25M commitment and new C-suite role show they're treating this as material to operations, not just PR damage control.

I appreciate that they responded quickly and seem to be taking concrete steps, but honestly, this makes me wonder what else they weren't paying attention to. As someone who's been buying their products for years because I trusted their brand values, I feel a bit betrayed that these issues existed in the first place. I'll probably wait to see what the audit actually finds and whether they follow through on their promises before I decide whether to keep shopping with them. The weekly updates are a good sign, but actions matter more than words at this point.

My relationship with EcoHarvest remains fundamentally transactional - I'm covering them as a story, not as a consumer. From a journalistic standpoint, this response actually makes them more interesting to follow because they've created multiple accountability touchpoints I can track. The real test will be whether they maintain this transparency when the initial media heat dies down - most companies revert to opacity once the spotlight moves elsewhere. I'll be particularly watching those weekly updates and whether the Chief Supply Chain Ethics Officer gets genuine authority or becomes a PR figurehead.

This response demonstrates appropriate procedural accountability, which is encouraging from a regulatory perspective. However, my trust would depend entirely on execution and compliance with their stated timelines and commitments. The 90-day audit timeline concerns me - comprehensive supply chain reviews typically require 6-12 months to be thorough. I'll be monitoring their weekly progress reports and the independence of the Deloitte audit scope. Their willingness to establish board-level oversight and public reporting creates enforceable accountability mechanisms that align with regulatory best practices.

Honestly, I'm torn. On one hand, this is exactly how a responsible company should respond - fast, transparent, with real money behind it. But as an employee, I'm also worried about what this says about our leadership's oversight in the first place. The fact that they're being so proactive gives me some confidence we can weather this, but I'll be watching those weekly updates closely to see if they follow through. My trust isn't broken, but it's definitely shaken.

From a competitive analysis standpoint, this response actually increases my professional respect for EcoHarvest's crisis management capabilities, even if I remain skeptical about their operational integrity.
